sentence: A troponin test measures proteins released when heart muscle is damaged, and a raised result does not always mean a heart attack.
note: MedlinePlus: troponin released when heart muscle damaged; NHS: raised troponin may have other causes

sentence: Troponin T and troponin I are proteins found in heart muscle.
They are released into the blood when the heart muscle is damaged, for example in a heart attack.
The more damage there is, the more troponin reaches the blood.
Clinicians mainly use the test to check whether a heart attack is happening or has recently happened.
It is typically ordered when someone has chest pain or other signs of a heart attack.
It can also be ordered for worsening angina without other signs of a heart attack, and to look for other causes of heart injury.
The NHS treats an ECG as an important early test in a suspected heart attack, and says it should be done within 10 minutes of arrival at hospital.
Blood tests look for troponin, which leaks slowly into the blood after damage to the heart.
Levels usually rise over hours, so testing is often repeated over several hours.
NICE guidance quoted by the NHS says a second troponin sample is usually taken a few hours after the first, unless the first is normal and the risk is judged low.
Newer high-sensitivity tests can detect a rise sooner after chest pain begins.
Normal levels some hours after symptoms began make a heart attack unlikely.
Very high levels most often mean a heart attack has occurred.
Raised levels do not always mean a heart attack, because other heart conditions can raise troponin.
A UK study reported by University Hospital Southampton found raised troponin in some people with unrelated conditions, so results need careful interpretation.
After a heart attack, levels may stay high for one to two weeks.
The ECG and troponin results together help to identify the type of heart attack.
A STEMI shows particular changes on the ECG.
An NSTEMI is found when the ECG does not show those changes but blood tests show heart damage.
The NHS advises calling 999 for chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw.
Severe difficulty breathing, pale, blue or grey lips or skin, and passing out also need a 999 call.
The NHS says not to drive to A&E, because the person on the 999 line gives advice on what to do.
